title: Shared vs. Dedicated AI Inference: Embed & Rerank
gist: Cohere argues that choosing between shared (consumption) and dedicated inference for Embed and Rerank depends on request shape, traffic pattern and utilization, not on headline price or requests per minute. Its illustrative A10-based break-evens range from about 4 requests/min for long-document embedding to tens of thousands for short query embedding.

insights.claim: Requests per minute is not a reliable sizing metric for embedding workloads, because a few large embedding requests can consume more compute than thousands of small search queries.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: When sizing AI inference spend, ask for tokens per request, not just RPM.
insights.quote: Request shape matters more than request volume alone.

insights.claim: A catalog-indexing embedding job (100 descriptions of ~200 tokens per request) is throughput-bound, while a single shopper query is latency-bound, so one model does two opposite jobs needing different infrastructure.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Batch and interactive embedding should be provisioned and priced separately.

insights.claim: Reranking cost scales with candidate count: moving from 20 to 50-100 candidates raises tokens per search from about 4,400 to about 22,000 with no change in user-visible search volume.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Retrieval-depth choices are a hidden driver of inference compute demand.
insights.locator: Reranking has a different request shape

insights.claim: Dedicated inference is generally more economical for sustained, predictable workloads, while consumption-based inference suits variable or bursty traffic.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Utilization, not peak load, decides which deployment model has the better cost.

insights.claim: Utilization consistency matters more than peak traffic: 10,000 requests/sec for 5 minutes a day has very different economics than 100 requests/sec constantly.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Idle provisioned GPUs are the main risk of dedicated deployments.
insights.quote: It's "How consistently can the infrastructure be utilized?"

insights.claim: In Cohere's illustrative analysis the same model at the same price has break-evens of ~4 req/min (100 texts x 1000 tokens), ~20 req/min (100 x 200 tokens), ~29 req/min (rerank 1 query + 50 docs) and tens of thousands req/min (short query).
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Break-evens span four orders of magnitude, so vendor 'rule of thumb' thresholds are unreliable.
insights.locator: The cost crossover depends on the workload

insights.claim: The break-evens assume a single hourly-billed NVIDIA A10 GPU, no negotiated discounts and 24x7 traffic; part-day workloads need higher request rates to reach the crossover.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Treat published break-evens as illustrative, and re-run them with your own pricing and hardware.
insights.locator: The cost crossover depends on the workload

insights.claim: A catalog embedding workload of only 30 requests per minute already exceeds its ~20 req/min break-even, so dedicated capacity is cheaper despite the modest request rate.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Small-looking workloads can still justify provisioned capacity.
insights.locator: The cost crossover depends on the workload

insights.claim: Many search applications end up using both: dedicated capacity for catalog indexing and consumption pricing for spiky end-user query traffic.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Hybrid deployment is the likely end state for retrieval stacks.

insights.claim: Maximum benchmark throughput is not usable capacity for interactive workloads; sizing must meet latency targets, which often requires headroom beyond peak demand.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Capacity plans based on peak throughput will under-provision latency-sensitive services.
insights.quote: Maximum throughput doesn't equal usable capacity

insights.claim: Larger rerank candidate sets increase documents processed per second while lowering searches served per second.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Retrieval-depth and capacity decisions trade off directly.
